subtitle: Midterm Important Subjective Questions (Solved)
topics: Functional Genomics, Gene Expression & Genome Informatics

subjective.question: (3 marks) Define genomics. How does genomics help in understanding genes?
subjective.answer: Genomics is the study of all the genes of an organism — the complete set of genetic material (the genome) — including their sequences, structure, organization and interactions. Genomics helps us to understand the functions of genes: by studying the whole genome instead of one gene at a time, we can learn what each gene does, how genes are switched on and off, and how they work together in health and disease.

subjective.question: (3 marks) Define a gene. Differentiate between gene families and gene clusters.
subjective.answer: A gene is a piece of DNA that contains the primary sequence needed to produce a functional biological product (a protein or a functional RNA). Gene families are groups of related genes descended from a common ancestral gene and having similar sequences and functions, e.g. the globin genes. Gene clusters are genes arranged together in groups along a chromosome; related genes may be organized as several clusters at different locations in the genome. In short, family refers to relatedness of the genes, while cluster refers to their physical grouping on the chromosome.

subjective.question: (3 marks) What are introns and exons? State the rule for the ends of an intron.
subjective.answer: Protein-coding genes of eukaryotes are split into coding regions called exons and non-coding intervening regions called introns. The introns are transcribed into the primary RNA transcript but are removed by splicing before translation, while the exons are joined together to form the mature mRNA. Almost every intron begins (at its 5' end) with the dinucleotide GT and ends (at its 3' end) with AG — this is known as the GT–AG rule.

subjective.question: (3 marks) Why do bacterial genes mostly lack introns? What is polycistronic mRNA?
subjective.answer: Bacterial (prokaryotic) genes are mostly continuous coding sequences without introns, because prokaryotes have compact genomes with high coding density and no nucleus, so transcription and translation occur together and there is no room or need for split genes. Polycistronic mRNA is the mRNA found in prokaryotes that encodes several proteins — it carries the coding sequences of a number of (usually related) genes in a single transcript, as in an operon, so several proteins are produced from one mRNA molecule.

subjective.question: (5 marks) Compare prokaryotic and eukaryotic genomes. (Any five differences)
subjective.answer: (1) Size and organization: prokaryotic genomes are small (bacteria and archaea mostly 1–6 Mb) and usually a single circular DNA molecule; eukaryotic genomes are much larger and divided among several linear chromosomes in a nucleus. (2) Introns: prokaryotic genes mostly lack introns; eukaryotic protein-coding genes contain introns. (3) Coding density: small (prokaryotic) genomes have high coding density with very little non-coding DNA, whereas eukaryotic genomes are full of repetitive DNA (simple repeats) and non-coding sequences. (4) RNA polymerase: prokaryotes have one type of RNA polymerase for all types of RNA; eukaryotes have three types. (5) mRNA: prokaryotic mRNA is polycistronic (encodes several proteins); eukaryotic mRNA is normally monocistronic (one protein). Overall, prokaryotic and eukaryotic genomes are significantly different from each other.

subjective.question: (5 marks) Comment on the statement: "Within each domain there is no systematic relationship between genome size and phenotype." Give the genome size ranges of viruses, bacteria/archaea and plants/animals in your answer.
subjective.answer: The statement means that a bigger genome does not mean a more complex organism — genome size alone cannot predict the phenotype or complexity of an organism within a domain (this is related to the C-value study). Genome sizes vary enormously: viral genomes are the smallest, from a few thousand to more than a hundred thousand nucleotides; most bacterial and archaeal genomes range from about 1 to 6 million base pairs (Mb); and most plants and animals have genomes greater than 100 Mb, with some exceeding 1000 Mb. Yet some simpler organisms have larger genomes than more complex ones, because much of the extra DNA is non-coding/repetitive. Because genomes are so large, useful information is hard to find in them, which is why genome informatics is needed.

subjective.question: (2 marks) What are telomeres? What type of DNA do they contain?
subjective.answer: Telomeres are the protective regions present at the ends of linear eukaryotic chromosomes. They consist of repetitive DNA — short DNA sequences repeated many times — which protect the chromosome ends from degradation and from being joined to other chromosomes, and they shorten slightly at each cell division.

subjective.question: (3 marks) What was the Human Genome Project? When was it completed and how long did it take?
subjective.answer: The Human Genome Project (HGP) was the international research programme whose goal was to determine the complete sequence of the human genome and to identify and map all of its genes. It was completed in 2003 and took 13 years of work by laboratories around the world.

subjective.question: (5 marks) Write the main steps of the Human Genome Project in order, and briefly explain each step.
subjective.answer: (1) Map construction (first step): genetic and physical maps of the genome are constructed to provide landmarks. (2) Clone selection (second step): overlapping clones (e.g. BAC clones) covering each chromosome are selected from libraries. (3) Sub-clone library construction: the selected large clones are broken into smaller sub-clones suitable for sequencing. (4) Random shotgun phase: the sub-clones are sequenced randomly. (5) Assembly and finishing: computer programs assemble the sequences into chromosomes and the gaps are closed, giving the complete genome sequence, which is then annotated.

subjective.question: (5 marks) What is the clone-by-clone (hierarchical shotgun) strategy of genome sequencing? How are BAC clones used to obtain the complete sequence of a chromosome?
subjective.answer: In the clone-by-clone strategy, the genome is first broken into large fragments that are cloned into vectors such as BACs (bacterial artificial chromosomes, which can carry inserts of about 300 kb and replicate in E. coli). The BAC clones are arranged into a clone contig map so that the position of every clone on the chromosome is known. Each mapped BAC clone is then sequenced by the shotgun method, and using the chromosomal map for the BAC clones, the BAC insert sequences are put together in the correct order to yield the complete chromosome sequence. Its advantage is that every sequence can be assigned to a known location, avoiding confusion between similar sequences from different places.

subjective.question: (3 marks) What is dideoxy (Sanger) sequencing? Why is it also called chain-termination sequencing?
subjective.answer: Dideoxy sequencing is the enzymatic method of DNA sequencing developed by Frederick Sanger, and it is the method used to sequence genomes in the Human Genome Project era. It uses dideoxynucleotides (ddNTPs), which lack the 3'-OH group needed to extend a growing DNA strand. Whenever a ddNTP is incorporated, synthesis stops, so a set of fragments ending at every position of the sequence is produced; separating these fragments by size reveals the sequence. Because each fragment's chain is terminated by a dideoxynucleotide, it is called chain-termination sequencing.

subjective.question: (3 marks) Write any four important findings of the Human Genome Project about the human genome.
subjective.answer: (1) Chromosome 1 has the most genes, while the Y chromosome has the fewest genes. (2) The mutation rate in males is about twice the mutation rate in females. (3) The human genome contains far fewer protein-coding genes than originally expected (about 20,000–25,000). (4) Approximately 99% of mouse genes have a homologue in the human genome, showing how much of our genome is shared with other mammals. (Any four such findings.)

subjective.question: (3 marks) What ethical and legal issues are raised by the Human Genome Project and by genetic information?
subjective.answer: The Human Genome Project raises complex ethical issues. Privacy and confidentiality of genetic information is an ethical and legal concern: a person's genome can reveal disease risks, so questions arise about who may have access to this information (employers, insurance companies), whether genetic discrimination may occur, who owns the genetic data, and how predictive genetic testing affects individuals and families psychologically and socially. These issues require laws and guidelines to protect individuals.

subjective.question: (2 marks) What is genome annotation?
subjective.answer: Genome annotation is the process of assigning identities and functions to sequences within the genome — that is, locating the genes in a sequenced genome and determining what each gene does. It is the step that converts raw sequence data into biologically useful information.

subjective.question: (3 marks) Why do we sequence genomes? Give any four reasons.
subjective.answer: We sequence genomes: (1) to understand the mechanisms of inherited diseases; (2) to understand infectious diseases and the genomes of pathogenic bacteria; (3) to identify genes and their functions; (4) to compare genomes of different species and understand evolution; and (5) to develop new diagnostic tests and drugs (personalized medicine). (Note: understanding metabolic diseases is not a standard stated aim in the course quiz bank — genomes are sequenced mainly for inherited and infectious disease mechanisms.)

subjective.question: (3 marks) Differentiate between genetic mapping and physical mapping.
subjective.answer: Genetic mapping (linkage mapping) locates genes/landmarks relative to each other based on recombination frequencies between polymorphic markers; distances are measured in centimorgans (cM) and the order reflects how often markers are inherited together. Physical mapping determines the actual physical positions of genes or DNA sequences on the chromosome, with distances measured in base pairs (bp/kb/Mb). Genetic mapping gives relative order by inheritance, while physical mapping gives real distances and positions.

subjective.question: (3 marks) What is cytogenetic mapping? How is it performed?
subjective.answer: Cytogenetic mapping is the localization of genes or DNA sequences on chromosomes by microscopic examination of stained chromosomes. Chromosomes are stained (e.g. G-banding) to produce a pattern of light and dark bands, and the position of a gene/sequence is described relative to these bands. It is the lowest-resolution type of physical map but links sequences directly to visible chromosomal regions.

subjective.question: (3 marks) What is FISH? What does it use, and what resolution can it achieve?
subjective.answer: FISH (Fluorescence In Situ Hybridization) is a type of (physical) mapping in which fluorescent probes — labelled DNA sequences complementary to the target — are hybridized to chromosomes spread on a slide, and the fluorescent signals are observed under a microscope to locate the target sequence. On less condensed (interphase) chromosomes, sequences in the range of about 5–700 kb apart may be resolved, giving much better resolution than metaphase chromosomes.

subjective.question: (3 marks) What is radiation hybrid mapping? What is it used for?
subjective.answer: Radiation hybrid mapping is a method used for high-resolution mapping of genomes. The DNA of the organism is broken into fragments by X-irradiation, and the fragments are rescued by fusing the irradiated cells with rodent (hamster) cells to form hybrid cell lines. The frequency with which two markers are retained together in the hybrids shows how close they are on the chromosome: markers that are close together tend to stay on the same fragment. It is used to order markers and build high-resolution maps of chromosomes.

subjective.question: (3 marks) What are polymorphic markers? Why are they required in a genetic mapping strategy?
subjective.answer: Polymorphic markers are DNA landmarks whose sequence differs between individuals (e.g. RFLPs, microsatellites/STRs and SNPs), so they exist in two or more forms (alleles) in a population. A genetic mapping strategy requires polymorphic markers because linkage can only be followed when a marker is heterozygous — i.e. the two copies inherited from the parents can be distinguished — allowing recombination between the marker and a gene to be detected and measured.

subjective.question: (2 marks) Name the types of physical maps in order of increasing resolution.
subjective.answer: Physical maps, in order of increasing resolution, are: (1) cytogenetic maps (lowest resolution), (2) radiation hybrid maps, (3) restriction maps, (4) clone contig / STS maps, and (5) the complete DNA sequence map (highest resolution). Types of physical maps are always presented in order of increasing resolution.

subjective.question: (5 marks) Why is yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) used as a model organism in genomics? Give the main features of its genome.
subjective.answer: Yeast is a simple, single-celled eukaryote that is cheap and easy to grow, has a short generation time, can be manipulated genetically with ease, and shares many basic cellular processes with higher eukaryotes — so findings in yeast apply to other eukaryotes. Its genome was completely sequenced by 1996, the first eukaryotic genome to be completed. Features of the yeast genome: the nuclear genome consists of 16 chromosomes; it is predicted to contain about 6,200 genes; and it has very few introns — only about 239 introns in the whole genome — showing its compact organization.

subjective.question: (3 marks) Write a short note on E. coli as a model organism in genomics.
subjective.answer: E. coli is a model organism for genome informatics (and for genome sequencing studies). It is a small, well-understood bacterium with a compact genome (about 4.6 Mb), it grows rapidly, and its genetics has been studied for decades, so its completely sequenced genome serves as a reference for developing and testing the computational (informatics) methods used to analyze genomes, and for understanding basic gene organization in prokaryotes.

subjective.question: (3 marks) Why is Arabidopsis thaliana a model plant for genome research? How many genes does its genome have and how many proteins do they encode?
subjective.answer: Arabidopsis thaliana is the model plant used for genome research because it has a small genome for a plant, a short life cycle, produces many seeds, and is easy to grow and transform in the laboratory, while still having the typical genes and processes of flowering plants. Its genome has about 27,000 genes, which encode about 35,000 proteins (because of alternative splicing, the number of proteins exceeds the number of genes).

subjective.question: (3 marks) What is comparative genomics? What does the fact that about 99% of mouse genes have a homologue in the human genome show?
subjective.answer: Comparative genomics is the comparison of genome sequences of different species to identify similarities and differences, conserved genes and regulatory elements, and to understand evolution and gene function. The fact that approximately 99% of mouse genes have a homologue (counterpart) in the human genome shows that mice and humans share almost the same set of genes, which is why the mouse is such a valuable model organism for studying human genes and diseases.

subjective.question: (5 marks) Define orthologues, paralogues, xenologues and analogues, with one line of explanation for each.
subjective.answer: These terms describe relationships between homologous genes/proteins. Orthologues: homologous genes in different species that evolved from a common ancestral gene by speciation and usually retain the same function. Paralogues: homologous genes within the same species/genome that arose by gene duplication and may evolve new functions. Xenologues: homologues that are related by horizontal (interspecies) transfer of genetic material — one of the homologues was acquired from another species. Analogues: non-homologous genes/proteins that have descended convergently from unrelated ancestors but perform a similar function. Highly conserved genes, in contrast, have changed very little over evolutionary time.

subjective.question: (2 marks) Drosophila is a model organism in which fields? With which group of animals does it show more similarities?
subjective.answer: Drosophila (the fruit fly) is a model organism in animal biology and genetics (developmental biology and genetics research). Despite being an insect, Drosophila has more similarities with mammals than with other invertebrate groups, which makes it useful for studying genes and development relevant to higher animals.

subjective.question: (3 marks) What is a DNA microarray? From which technique did the microarray technology evolve?
subjective.answer: A DNA microarray (DNA chip) is a solid surface (glass slide or chip) on which thousands of known DNA sequences (probes) are fixed in an ordered grid; a labelled sample is hybridized to it so that thousands of genes can be studied in a single experiment. Microarray technology evolved from Southern blotting, in which fragmented DNA is attached to a substrate (membrane) and then probed with a known DNA sequence — the microarray is a miniaturized, high-throughput form of this hybridization principle.

subjective.question: (2 marks) What is the biggest advantage of microarray technology?
subjective.answer: The biggest advantage of microarrays is that they provide data for thousands of genes simultaneously in a single experiment — gene expression profiling can be monitored for thousands of genes at the same time, instead of studying one gene at a time.

subjective.question: (5 marks) Differentiate between spotted DNA arrays and cartridge-based (expression) microarrays. (Any five points)
subjective.answer: (1) Construction: in spotted arrays, probe DNA is deposited (spotted) onto a glass slide, the probes being loaded by capillary action in a spotting pin; cartridge-based chips have high-density arrays of DNA oligonucleotides synthesized inside a plastic housing/cartridge. (2) Samples per chip: a spotted array can compare two samples on the same slide; a cartridge chip follows 'one sample = one chip' (e.g. Affymetrix, Agilent, Applied Biosystems). (3) Labelling: spotted arrays use two fluorescent dyes, Cy3 and Cy5, for the two samples on the same slide; cartridge-based expression arrays use fluorescently tagged biotinylated cRNA from a single sample. (4) Probe type: spotted arrays generally use longer DNA (cDNA) probes; cartridge chips use short oligonucleotides. (5) Use: cartridge-based chips are generally used with expression and DNA arrays in standardized commercial systems, while spotted arrays are commonly custom-made in laboratories. (Any five points.)

subjective.question: (3 marks) How is probe DNA loaded onto a spotted microarray slide, and how does a cartridge-based expression microarray experiment proceed?
subjective.answer: In spotted arrays, the probe DNA is loaded onto the slide by capillary action — the spotting pin picks up DNA solution by capillary action and deposits a tiny spot at a defined position, building up the grid of probes. In a cartridge-based expression microarray, cRNA is prepared from the sample's mRNA, tagged with biotin and a fluorescent label, and hybridized inside the sealed plastic cartridge containing the high-density oligonucleotide array; after washing, the fluorescence at each spot is scanned — one sample is processed on one chip.

subjective.question: (3 marks) Write any four applications of DNA microarrays. Why can a DNA microarray NOT be used for the analysis of protein function?
subjective.answer: Applications: (1) assessment/measurement of gene expression levels (expression profiling); (2) evaluation of microRNA levels; (3) discovery of new genes; (4) genotyping and detection of mutations/SNPs, and comparative genomic hybridization to detect copy-number changes. A DNA microarray cannot be used for analysis of protein function because it measures nucleic acids (DNA/RNA) by hybridization — it tells us about gene sequences and their expression levels, not about the proteins themselves or what the proteins do.

subjective.question: (3 marks) Name and briefly describe the types of microarrays.
subjective.answer: The main types are: (1) DNA microarrays — arrays of DNA probes used to study gene sequences and expression; (2) Comparative Genomic Hybridization (CGH) arrays — used to compare genomes and detect gains/losses (copy-number variations) of DNA; (3) Exon arrays — probes target individual exons, allowing study of alternative splicing and expression at exon level. (VNTR arrays are not a type of microarray.) Microarrays may also be classified by format into spotted arrays and cartridge-based chips.

subjective.question: (3 marks) What are methylation arrays? What do they help us to study?
subjective.answer: Methylation arrays are microarrays designed to determine which regions of DNA are methylated across the genome — i.e. they measure the methylation status of many CpG sites at once. Determining which regions of DNA are methylated ultimately helps in the study of epigenetics — the heritable changes in gene activity that do not involve changes in the DNA sequence — including gene silencing and the role of methylation in development and disease.

subjective.topic: Functional Genomics, Gene Expression & Genome Informatics
subjective.question: (3 marks) Differentiate between structural genomics and functional genomics.
subjective.answer: Structural genomics deals with the physical nature of the genome — determining genome sequences, the distinct components of genomes, gene structure and organization, and genome maps. Functional genomics analyzes all genes in genomes to determine their functions and their gene control and expression — i.e. what the genes do, when they are expressed and how they are regulated, using genome-wide approaches such as microarrays and abundance/complexity studies of mRNA.

subjective.topic: Functional Genomics, Gene Expression & Genome Informatics
subjective.question: (3 marks) What is population genomics? What does it study?
subjective.answer: Population genomics is the study of genomes of a specific population — the large-scale comparison of DNA sequences within and between populations. It studies the genetic diversity of populations and gives new insights into disease susceptibility and drug response in different groups. (Comparing gene numbers between species is comparative genomics, not population genomics.)

subjective.topic: Functional Genomics, Gene Expression & Genome Informatics
subjective.question: (3 marks) What is transcription? What are transcription factors and where do they bind?
subjective.answer: Transcription is the process by which cells express their genes: the DNA sequence of a gene is copied into RNA (mRNA) by the enzyme RNA polymerase. Transcription factors are proteins that bind to specific DNA sequences (promoter/enhancer regions) and help to control gene expression — they regulate the initiation and rate of transcription by assisting or blocking the binding of RNA polymerase.

subjective.topic: Functional Genomics, Gene Expression & Genome Informatics
subjective.question: (2 marks) How many types of RNA polymerase are present in prokaryotes and in eukaryotes?
subjective.answer: Prokaryotes have only one type of RNA polymerase, which synthesizes all types of RNA. Eukaryotes have three types of RNA polymerase (RNA polymerase I, II and III), each responsible for transcribing a different set of genes/RNAs.

subjective.topic: Functional Genomics, Gene Expression & Genome Informatics
subjective.question: (3 marks) What is metagenomics? Which molecule is used in metagenomics to examine phylogenetic diversity?
subjective.answer: Metagenomics is the study of genetic material recovered directly from environmental samples (e.g. soil, water, gut contents), examining the genomes of all the microorganisms present in that environment together, without culturing them individually. The phylogenetic diversity of the community is examined using the 16S rRNA gene, whose sequence varies between species and is the standard marker for identifying and classifying bacteria in such samples.

subjective.topic: Functional Genomics, Gene Expression & Genome Informatics
subjective.question: (3 marks) What is miRNA? Name the enzymes that process it and the enzyme class they belong to.
subjective.answer: miRNA (microRNA) is a small non-coding RNA that regulates gene expression by silencing target mRNAs. It originates from single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) transcripts that fold into a hairpin secondary structure. The hairpin is processed by two enzymes: Drosha (in the nucleus) and Dicer (in the cytoplasm). Both Drosha and Dicer are RNase III enzymes.

subjective.topic: Functional Genomics, Gene Expression & Genome Informatics
subjective.question: (3 marks) What is Ensembl? Which organizations run it? Name one other genome browser and its use.
subjective.answer: Ensembl is a genome browser/database project that provides annotated genome data for vertebrates and other species. It is a joint project between three organizations: EMBL (European Molecular Biology Laboratory), EBI (European Bioinformatics Institute) and WTSI (Wellcome Trust Sanger Institute). Another example is the UCSC Genome Browser: researchers can use it to find information in the genomes that have been sequenced, viewing genes, sequences and annotations along the chromosomes.

subjective.topic: Functional Genomics, Gene Expression & Genome Informatics
subjective.question: (2 marks) Describe the human mitochondrial genome. What is the size of the animal mitochondrial genome?
subjective.answer: The human mitochondrial genome is circular and double-stranded DNA, present in the mitochondria rather than the nucleus, and inherited maternally. The mitochondrial genome in animals is very small, about 15–16 kb in size (the marked answer in the course quiz is 15–16 kb), containing only 37 genes.
